newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban protest non-invitation to summit.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban protest non-invitation to summit.

text.p: The Taleban administration in the Afghan capital Kabul protested on Tuesday at being left out of a 10-country regional summit designed to improve economic ties.
A Taleban statement urged the secretary general of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) to review the policy of excluding the Taleban.

"The fifth summit of ECO member countries will be held without the participation of the real representatives of the Islamic State of Afghanistan, which will severely damage ECO's prestige," said a message from the Taleban-controlled foreign ministry to the secretary general of ECO.
"We ask you to review your current policies as a non- political organisation," the message said.
The 10 members of the ECO are Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
The group is meeting in Ashgabat, capital of Turkmenistan, to discuss options for exporting Central Asia's huge oil and gas resources to the outside world.

The Taleban, who control two-thirds of Afghanistan, have yet to be recognised as the legitimate government by any nation or international body. A representative of the government ousted by the Taleban from Kabul last September has been invited to represent Afghanistan at the Ashgabat conference.
One of the options under consideration by the conference is to build a gas pipeline through Afghanistan to the energy-hungry sub-continent.
The Afghan part of the proposed route is currently under the control of the Taleban.
Turkmenistan, which has most to gain if the proposed pipeline goes ahead, has performed a delicate balancing act between the conflicting priorities of its neighbours.
As the only Central Asian state to share a border with Taleban-controlled Afghanistan, Turkmenistan has been careful not to offend the purist militia.

The other four Central Asian states and Russia have held a number of meetings to come up with a coordinated policy to cope with what they perceive as the threat the Taleban would present should they succeed in taking the rest of the country.
The Taleban leadership have denied that they have any extra-territorial ambitions in Central Asia.

The Turkmen authorities have also cultivated ties with their other southern neighbour Iran, which the Taleban accuses of helping the Afghan opposition. The Iranians are keen to see the pipeline run through their territory.

Two consortia are already lining up to build the $2.5-billion pipeline through Afghanistan. One, led by Argentine energy independent Bridas, said on May 4 that it hoped to sign a deal with the Taleban authorities within 30 days.
Bridas has said that it will proceed even without a final solution to the conflict in Afghanistan.
The other consortium is led by Unocal of the United States and Delta Oil of Saudi Arabia.
